steps.action: Pose the question of whether the large and usually overlooked diversity of earthquake generation models in PSHA studies can be evaluated objectively.
steps.quote: there is also a large diversity on the earthquake generation models

steps.action: State the elastic-rebound premise: models whose moment release exceeds or falls far below the measured or estimated strain accumulation rate are suspicious.
steps.quote: the earthquake generation models used in PSHA that exceed that rate or that are far below should be considered suspicious

steps.action: Set aside gravitational potential energy (and GIA) as a strain source for W and SW Iberia on the basis of the authors' earlier work, and assume only tectonic horizontal strain drives earthquakes.
steps.quote: they conclude that GPE is a second-order effect that is mostly identified in high-relief areas

steps.action: Compile the published recurrence parameters of five PSHA studies (EC8, ERSTA, SHARE min/med/max, QREN, 32 VF2007 logic-tree branches) for the Lower Tagus Valley and 1755 source zones (Tables 1-4).
steps.quote: we will use the published parameters to make a sanity check

steps.action: Build the simple rule-of-thumb test: convert cumulative seismic moment from the DTGR law into slip rate on a single representative fault (Eq. 4, Fig. 5).
steps.quote: a simplified seismic generation model is used, with seismic strain concentrated on a single fault, representative of the zone under study

steps.action: Fix the test parameters per zone (shear modulus, seismogenic thickness 20 or 60 km, fault length, dip, coupling c = 1) as conservative values giving lower limits (Table 5).
steps.quote: must be inferred from our best knowledge on the source areas

steps.action: Expand the 32 discrete VF2007 logic-tree branches into a continuous slip-rate distribution by Monte Carlo sampling of a and b, and pick five representative scenarios by 20 % probability classes (Figs. 6-7).
steps.quote: We will expand the resulting discrete probability distribution into a continuous probability distribution through a Monte Carlo simulation

steps.action: Take the long-term lithospheric deformation of SW Iberia from the authors' earlier SHELLS neotectonic finite-element model (Neres et al., 2016).
steps.quote: That work was performed for the Africa–Eurasia plate boundary

steps.action: Modify Bird's long-term seismicity code to use source zones and the PSHA recurrence parameters instead of plate-boundary classes, after fitting each DTGR law to a tapered G-R law.
steps.quote: Firstly, we introduced the parametrization of zones, instead of plate boundaries.

steps.action: Check the DTGR-to-TGR conversion by comparing total seismic moment release of the original and fitted laws (details in Supplement S3).
steps.quote: The quality of the fit was assessed by comparing the total seismic moment release computed for both models, DTGR and fitted TGR.

steps.action: Compute the seismic slip rate implied by each PSHA model in both zones (Tables 8-9).
steps.quote: This test consisted in computing the fault slip rate that would explain the seismicity from the earthquake recurrence models proposed for PSHA

steps.action: Assemble published plate kinematics, GNSS velocity fields and geological fault slip rates for W and SW Iberia as the kinematic reference.
steps.quote: Palano et al. (2015) analysis of GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) data showed in SW Iberia a gradient in the measured velocities

steps.action: Set acceptance bounds: upper limits of 1 mm/yr (LTV) and 4 mm/yr (1755 zone); lower suspicion limits of 0.1 and 0.5 mm/yr.
steps.quote: we assume 1 mm yr - 1 as a reasonable kinematic reference value for the simple sanity check

steps.action: Convert the neotectonic deformation into long-term seismicity rates per magnitude class and moment rates for each zone, assuming perfect coupling (Tables 10-11).
steps.quote: lithospheric deformation can be converted to earthquake rates on the source zones used for PSHA

steps.action: Compare each PSHA model with the long-term seismicity estimate as a TGR/LTS ratio, read as required coupling; ratios near or above 1, or below 0.1, are suspect (Tables 10-12).
steps.quote: These ratios should be considered suspect if they are close to 1 or greater than 1

steps.action: Flag as suspect EC8, ERSTA and the SHARE variants (excess) and QREN (deficit) in the LTV zone; flag EC8, ERSTA (excess), SHAREmax, QREN and four VF2007 scenarios in the 1755 zone.
steps.quote: clearly identifies three models with excessive earthquake generation

steps.action: Cross-check the simple test against the complex neotectonic test: the two classifications agree on 20 of 22 models.
steps.quote: the simplified consistency check evaluation agrees with the more elaborate one on 20 out of the 22 PSHA earthquake generation models

steps.action: Vary the inputs: Monte Carlo propagation of a and b uncertainty over all 32 VF2007 models (10 % excess in LTV, 40 % deficit in the 1755 zone), and two comparison indicators (per-magnitude activity ratio and moment-rate ratio) that give the same classification.
steps.quote: Using Monte Carlo simulation to account for uncertainties in the DTGR law parameters, 10 % of those models generated earthquakes in excess.

steps.action: Keep both tests as usable consistency checks for PSHA in slowly deforming regions and recommend using their outcome to weight logic-tree branches.
steps.quote: Both tests can be used to assess the consistency of PSHA models.

No; long-term strain comes from GNSS and geology onshore and only from a neotectonic model offshore.

end.claim: Two consistency tests (slip on a typical fault against plate and GNSS kinematics; neotectonic long-term seismicity against PSHA rates) classify PSHA earthquake generation models consistently (20 of 22 agree) and flag several published SW Iberia models as producing too many or too few earthquakes.

decisive_move.sentence: Adapting the long-term seismicity code to PSHA source zones and their recurrence parameters turned an inherited neotectonic deformation model into a quantitative reference against which each published model could be scored.

gates.evidence: No new data were acquired. The moment-budget premise (§1 ¶7) directed which published parameters, geodetic data and neotectonic outputs were assembled, so the action gate is partly met. Each model could have passed or failed the slip-rate and ratio bounds (§5.1 ¶8, §5.2 ¶1), and the simple test could have disagreed with the complex one (§5.3 ¶3), so the claim gate is met. Nothing is reported as fixed before results were seen: the thresholds are stated in the results section, and only the rule for selecting the five VF2007 scenarios by 20 % classes is stated in advance (§4.2 ¶1).

novelty_claims.quote: We propose two consistency tests to address the variability of earthquake generation models found in PSHA studies
We think that the novelty of our approach rests in determining the earthquake rates from a neotectonics model

limits: Sub-claims and their statuses: (a) Specific models (EC8, ERSTA, SHARE variants, QREN, four VF2007 scenarios in the 1755 zone) are suspect. This is an exclusion, but only relative to judgment-set thresholds, so at most best_explanation. (b) The suggested explanation for poor performance in the 1755 zone (poor geological control) is offered without a test (§5.3 ¶3). (c) The abstract says the analysis allowed a downgrade of model weights, but no reweighted hazard is computed in the paper. The neotectonic reference (Neres et al., 2016) is the authors' own earlier work and is not re-validated here. Sensitivity to thickness, coupling, dip and length is argued algebraically and left to the reader (§5.3 ¶5); it is not run. Inference: internal inconsistencies weaken the reported tallies. The text names 'three models' but lists four (§5.3 ¶1). It writes 'VF2002' for VF2007 (§5.3 ¶2). It says 'only three' pass both tests in the 1755 zone but '4 of 11' pass the complex test (§5.3 ¶2-3). Table 9 shows some mmax+0.5 slip rates below the mmax values despite larger moment rates. The Supplement (Eq. S4, Sect. S3) was not supplied, so the fit-quality check is coded from the main-text description. Composition is none_fits: the walk screens pre-existing rival models with a shared moment-budget test, which resembles strong_inference. But no survivor is refined, the bounds are set by judgment, and the paper is framed as a method proposal, so capability_first does not fit either.

disagreements.target: Mulargia et al. (2017), proposal to abandon PSHA
disagreements.support: The authors argue on societal grounds that PSHA will remain in use and offer physical consistency tests to improve it, not new evidence against the critique.
disagreements.quote: We do not follow Mulargia et al.'s (2017) proposal to completely abandon PSHA

disagreements.target: EC8, ERSTA and SHARE recurrence models for the Lower Tagus Valley
disagreements.support: Their moment release exceeds the neotectonic long-term seismicity (ratios 1.05-2.86) and, in the simple test, approaches or exceeds the 1 mm/yr geodetic bound.
disagreements.quote: clearly identifies three models with excessive earthquake generation

disagreements.support: Its slip rate (0.06 mm/yr in LTV) and ratio (0.06-0.13) imply implausibly low seismic coupling in both zones.
disagreements.quote: The QREN model shows too little earthquake generation, confirmed by both sanity checks, simple and complex.

disagreements.target: EC8 and ERSTA models for the 1755 source zone
disagreements.support: Their ratios to the long-term seismicity rates are 1.16 and 3.92, and the ERSTA slip rate of 14.4 mm/yr exceeds the 4 mm/yr plate convergence.
disagreements.quote: The complex consistency test identifies scenarios EC8 and ERSTA as being clearly excessive in earthquake generation

disagreements.target: Kinematic deformation modelling (Bird, 2009; Carafa et al., 2020) for offshore domains
disagreements.support: The authors argue that offshore the choice of faults controls where deformation localizes and leaves no independent data for testing; no comparison is run.
disagreements.quote: it does not allow consistent estimation of the offshore long-term deformation

disagreements.target: Mixed fault-and-zone source model (Rivas-Medina et al., 2018)
disagreements.support: Fault geometry and activity in W and SW Iberia are too poorly known, as described in Sect. 2.
disagreements.quote: This is an exceptional case that cannot be extended to the whole W and SW Iberia.

disagreements.target: Community attribution of PSHA divergence to ground motion prediction equations
disagreements.support: The authors point to the large diversity of earthquake generation models (Fig. 3) as a second, overlooked source of divergence.
disagreements.quote: This large diversity is usually ascribed to the large uncertainty on the second term of Eq.

disagreements.target: Time ergodicity assumption in slowly deforming regions
disagreements.support: Cites the New Madrid case (Newman et al., 1999) as evidence that the assumption can fail.
disagreements.quote: The New Madrid events show that time ergodicity, a common assumption for earthquake generation in slowly deforming regions, can fail dramatically.

alternatives_considered.alternatives: kinematic modelling by inversion of GPS and stress data
alternatives_considered.reason: kinematic models rarely explain mechanisms, leave no independent data for testing, and cannot estimate offshore deformation consistently

alternatives_considered.chosen: perfect seismic coupling c = 1 (results as lower limits)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: c < 1, varying from 0.05 to 1.0 per Bird and Kagan (2004)

alternatives_considered.chosen: zone-specific L, H = 20 or 60 km, mu, dip (Table 5)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: other values of length and thickness
alternatives_considered.reason: best knowledge of the source areas; the values are conservative

alternatives_considered.chosen: tapered Gutenberg-Richter law fitted to each published DTGR law
alternatives_considered.alternatives: double truncated Gutenberg-Richter law as published
alternatives_considered.reason: the long-term seismicity code uses the TGR law

alternatives_considered.chosen: five representative VF2007 scenarios, one per 20 % probability class
alternatives_considered.reason: representative of the continuous slip-rate distribution

alternatives_considered.chosen: both indicators: activity ratio per magnitude class and moment-rate ratio

alternatives_considered.alternatives: mixed fault and zone sources; more detailed source parametrization
alternatives_considered.reason: onshore fault slip rates are very low and offshore seismicity has no clear link to mapped faults
